extracted.intended_audience: researchers planning or conducting empirical studies who want to preregister (authors, students, and those submitting to journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, updating, and reporting preregistrations for empirical research (confirmatory and exploratory), including special cases such as existing data, split samples, longitudinal studies, embargoes, and interactions with peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify research plan in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: When you preregister your research, you're simply specifying your research plan in advance of your study and submitting it to a registry. Preregistering creates a specific plan for the upcoming study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preregistration helps distinguish planned from unplanned work, improving transparency and credibility. Use OSF help guides and available templates. Phrase things clearly to enable readers to see what was planned prior to data analysis. 'A plan, not a prison'—preregistration is meant to guide transparency rather than forbid changes if disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish confirmatory vs exploratory analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned Research: Most often, this is 'confirmatory' research. Unplanned Research: Most often, this is exploratory research. Preregistration distinguishes confirmatory and exploratory analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirmatory analyses aim to minimize Type I errors and require clear, specific hypotheses and tests; exploratory analyses are hypothesis-generating and require replication to be confirmed. Make the distinction explicit in reports (e.g., separate confirmatory and exploratory results sections). At least one confirmatory test must be specified in each preregistration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report all results from preregistered analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes. The central aims of preregistration are to distinguish confirmatory and exploratory analyses in order to retain the validity of their statistical inferences. Selective reporting of planned analyses is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not selectively report only significant results from your preregistered plan. If many tests were planned, consider reducing number of confirmatory tests or include multiple-test adjustments. If you dismiss preregistered analyses as inappropriate in retrospect, do so explicitly and transparently so readers can evaluate the remaining confirmatory results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret all preregistered results (avoid selective interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes. Selective interpretation of pre-planned analyses can disrupt the diagnosticity of statistical inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many planned tests were conducted and only significant ones are discussed, interpretations may be misleading. To reduce bias, focus confirmatory designs on a small number of key tests or include corrections for multiple testing. Explicitly state if you interpret only a subset and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow exploratory analyses but label them
rubrics_metrics.description: No. Preregistration distinguishes confirmatory and exploratory analyses. Exploratory analysis is very important for discovery and hypothesis generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may conduct unplanned/exploratory analyses, but they must be clearly labeled as exploratory or data-driven; p-values from exploratory analyses are less diagnostic and require subsequent confirmatory testing with new data.

rubrics_metrics.name: At least one confirmatory test required
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one confirmatory test must be specified in each preregistration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the preregistration contains some genuine confirmatory content. If none exists, the registration is purely exploratory and should be reported as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and certification when using existing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories for which preregistration may still use existing data: registration prior to collection of data; prior to any human observation of the data; prior to access to the data; prior to analysis of the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each timing category has different certification requirements: certify that data do not exist; certify that data exist but have not been quantified/observed and explain how; certify who has accessed data and justify how prior access does not compromise confirmatory nature; or certify that no analysis related to the Research Plan has been conducted. Provide justifications that reviewers can evaluate for potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certify prior knowledge/access for archival/public data
rubrics_metrics.description: For preregistering studies using archival or public research data, it is important to disclose your prior knowledge and exposure to the data at the time of registering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about what you knew to help readers assess potential bias. Too much prior knowledge can diminish the bias-mitigation value of preregistration. Disclose previous analyses, summary statistics seen, or other exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold out data / split-sample strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold out data-sets or split samples: randomly split off some 'real' data for exploration and use reserved portion for confirmation. The reusable holdout and split-sample strategies preserve validity in adaptive analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split-sample strategies reduce sample for confirmatory analysis but increase credibility. Use model training/validation analogy. References and example papers are provided. Useful when you cannot fully prespecify models without exploratory work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional analyses via decision-tree (IF-THEN rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmatory analyses can be conditional. A pre-analysis plan might specify preconditions for certain analysis strategies and what alternative analysis will be performed if those conditions are not met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a 'decision-tree' with logical IF-THEN rules (e.g., test normality → if violated use nonparametric test). Provide examples and link to example decision trees. This makes conditional choices transparent while preserving confirmatory status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent Changes when updating preregistration
rubrics_metrics.description: When changes occur in your project after the registration is finalized, you have two options: create a new preregistration and withdraw the original, or start a Transparent Changes document uploaded to the OSF project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option 1 (create new preregistration + withdraw original) is recommended for serious errors or if you haven't started data collection; include a withdrawal note explaining rationale and link to new registration. Option 2 (Transparent Changes doc) is recommended if you've already begun the study. Use provided template and be explicit about changes when reporting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short registration process: allowed updates before analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Updates or amendments to a preregistration are permissible (in most cases) prior to analyzing the data (up until the outcomes of the study are known).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may update to use a better technique before analyzing data. It is not okay to update after results of initial analyses are known if changes shift analyses toward mining for significance—such post-hoc changes must be labeled as exploratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation within 48 hours and contributor confirmation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If your preregistration on the OSF is less than 48 hours old and has not yet been confirmed by its contributors, you can cancel it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See OSF details for cancellation flow. This is for very recent, unconfirmed registrations only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo and withdrawal policies
rubrics_metrics.description: You may embargo your preregistration plan for up to 4 years. All registrations eventually become public. It is possible to withdraw your preregistration, but a notification of the withdrawal will be public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargoes delay public disclosure to reduce 'file-drawer' effects while allowing future claims to be preserved. You may end an embargo early. Withdrawal leaves a public notice—transparency is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method detail: replicability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of detail should be enough for an interested reader to be able to replicate the methods of the original study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the perspective of future readers: include necessary methodological and analytic details for replication or extension, but be concise—overly long preregistrations are less likely to be read in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify variables used in confirmatory tests
rubrics_metrics.description: If the variables will be used in testing the preregistered hypotheses, then you must define them in the preregistration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variables not used for preregistered hypotheses need not be listed, though including them can aid clarity if they will be used for exploratory or data-driven analyses. At minimum, define variables tied to confirmatory tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymized links for peer review and anonymity cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: You can submit anonymized view-only links for peer review. Be sure that any attached files or answers to registration questions do not contain any identifying information (including file titles!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymized view-only links remove the Author section of the form but cannot redact identifying info inside uploaded files. Manually remove or anonymize identifying details in files before sharing to preserve double-blind review if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered Reports vs preregistration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered Reports are a publication format in which the preregistered plan undergoes peer review in advance of observing research outcomes; successful review can grant 'in principle acceptance' (IPA) guaranteeing publication conditional on following accepted methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After IPA, preserve the accepted research plan; journals may preserve it or you can register via the OSF RR workflow (https://osf.io/rr). Registered Reports involve editorial oversight and peer review of the research plan itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance limits: when preregistration fits poorly
rubrics_metrics.description: There are research circumstances that present challenges to preregistration: studies not conducting statistical inference testing, qualitative research, certain observational studies, and field studies with unpredictable events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether standard preregistration models apply; if not, contact COS to develop appropriate processes. For field studies, include contingencies in advance and use pilot trials or additional planning to identify possible data-collection contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal studies and preregistration pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: In longitudinal studies with previous rounds of data, forthcoming rounds are likely correlated to previous rounds, making confirmatory preregistration challenging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: partner with colleagues who haven't seen previous summaries, use unused variables for new analyses, reserve hold-out confirmatory sets, or acknowledge that some analyses must be exploratory. Be transparent about what was known prior to registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple papers from a single data collection: use components and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple planned studies come from one data collection effort, balance making a clear connection from the final paper to the preregistered plan and ensuring complete context is reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize large projects using OSF 'components' (sub-projects) for separate analysis plans, disclose that papers are part of a larger study, and consider parsing data collection into component preregistrations decided in a data-independent manner to avoid perceived selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to reviewers/editors regarding preregistered plans
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers or editors request removal of preregistered analyses, additional tests, or question separate reporting of preregistered analyses, authors should defend transparent reporting and distinguish confirmatory vs additional analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible responses: insist that preregistered analyses remain because removing null results perpetuates publication bias; clarify preregistration certification date and provide OSF URL; accept additional tests but label them as non-preregistered. If reviewers suggest validity concerns about a preregistered test, keep it but discuss limitations in the discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use preregistration to stake claim and credit ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Preregistration allows you to stake your claim to your ideas earlier and is an easy way to plan for better research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are encouraged to use preregistration language verbatim in your later paper and to cite the preregistration for clarity and discoverability; change tense or quote to address self-plagiarism concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to preregister (timing guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Can You Preregister? Right before your next round of data collection; after you are asked to collect more data in peer review; before you begin analysis of an existing data set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preregister whenever you can define a confirmatory plan before observing the outcomes that will be used in those analyses. For existing data, follow the timing/certification categories and disclose prior knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical resources and templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Templates of many preregistration forms are available; primers, checklists for complete analysis plans and reporting, and help docs to register on OSF are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available templates, workshops, checklists, and example preregistrations curated by OSF and partners (e.g., UK Reproducibility Network materials) to improve completeness and clarity of preregistrations.
